To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
calcium is distributed in five phases, that inotropic changes are associated with calcium redistribution, and that prolonged low sodium perfusion results in a calcium binding that is irreversible.

the inotropism produced by low sodium perfusion of the dog papillary muscles is due to the net accumulation of Ca++ in the muscle, that the net accumulation of muscle Ca++ occurs in two phases, the first of which is rapidly exchangeable and the second of which is irreversibly bound to the tissue, and that the exchangeable phase of muscle Ca++ represents the Ca++ content in the specialized calcium transport system.
calcium exchange in the dog heart muscle is complex and that the inotropic effects of low sodium perfusate are related to calcium movements.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a study of calcium distribution in vascularly perfused dog papillary muscle and its relationship to the inotropic state.
the distribution of calcium in the dog ventricle and the effects of changes in the extracellular sodium concentration on calcium distribution and the contractile state of the ventricle.
a kinetic description of calcium distribution in dog ventricular muscle.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the inotropic effect of sodium concentration on the heart is due to a change in the Ca++ content (and hence the Ca++ flux) of the “specialzed system.” This effect of low sodium concentration on the Ca++ content is not due to a change of calcium influx or efflux but rather to a change in a calcium compartment of the cell.
the Ca++ movements in this preparation were complex and that the inotropic effect of low sodium perfusions was related to a change in Ca++ concentration in the muscle.

(1) calcium exchange in the dog papillar muscle can be described kinetically in terms of at least five phases, and (2) the “specialized calcium transport system” may represent the major intracellular store of calcium and the site of control of intracellular Ca++ concentration.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
calcium is distributed among at least four kinetically distinct pools, one of which may be controlled by sodium and which is associated with the inotropy of contraction.
calcium movements in muscle are complex and that a complete understanding of these movements will require further study of the interrelations of calcium and sodium in the muscle.
the inotropic effects of Na+ and Ca++ in this preparation may be explained by a Na+-Ca++ exchange in a system other than the sarcoplasmic reticular system.
The main takeaway from our work is that
calcium is not just in the sarcoplasmic reticular space but is also in the cytoplasm and in the interstitial space.
calcium is not a static element in the cell.
the inotropic effect of sodium is not a simple function of calcium concentration.
